Interactive introductory distance sampling training

The University of St Andrews has been training people in design and analysis of distance sampling studies for decades.  Perhaps you've wanted to attend but could not get permission for travel to Scotland or the scheduling of workshops in August conflicted with your field work. 👨‍🌾

We are offering the training workshop in 10 two-hour blocks in early May.  You will be invited to interact in short lectures on distance sampling principles. 👩‍🎓 Exercises analysing data sets in R will reinforce those principles and the lecturer will be available to assist during the practical session via screen sharing.  The block will conclude with a summary of the exercise and question/answer session for both lecture and exercise. 💻  You can participate in polls during the workshop to assess your comprehension of topics discussed. 🤔

The workshop will be delivered using Zoom web conferencing software along with R-Studio "in the cloud".☁️ You will need (free) accounts for both pieces of software. I encourage you to experiment with Zoom (at https://zoom.us) and https://rstudio.cloud before the course begins. 👩‍💻  There will be a training session prior to the first meeting on 04 May.

Companion online training workshops

We are planning additional advanced distance sampling workshops later this summer.  These workshops (spatial modelling delivery in early June and mark-recapture distance sampling delivery in late August) will require knowledge of basic distance sampling principles derived from this introductory training workshop.

Important details

    Workshop dates and time: 04-15 May 2020; 1700-1900 British summer time (1200-1400 EDT, 0900-1100 PDT) 🕰️
    Registration deadline:  17 April 2020📅
    Enrolment limit: 15
    Cost: 200 British pounds 💵
    What is included: Lectures, exercises, code, data all available online📃

Further details are available at the CREEM website

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/distance-live-online-workshops/

At this page you will find a link to the St Andrews online shop where you a) register and b) make payment.

Feel free to contact me with questions (eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk). Information regarding all distance sampling workshops can be found at

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/workshops/
Workshops | CREEM <https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/workshops/>
Current Workshops: Distance Live online workshop 17th-28th February 2020.Registration is now closed. Information about the Distance workshops in St Andrews in August 2020 is available here.

I have a project regarding cetacean sightings using distance sampling. During the data collection, we also collected weather variables every effort update. I would like to make a summary_ds table of all these different models. However, I'm having issues adding these formulae to the model, as the only one working is:

> bal.sz.ds <- ds(fram.var, truncation = 3000, formula = ~size, key = "hr")

when I use the other variables such as:

> bal.obs.ds <- ds(fram.var, truncation = "15%", formula = ~observer, key = "hr")

no models could be fitted!

Is this a problem with the way the variables are formulated? Are number of covariates limited in the formulae? I would love to have:

> bal.mix.ds <- ds(fram.var, truncation = "15%", key = "hr", formula = ~observer + size + weather) #or something of the sort

Thank you for your help!

Hope everyone is healthy in these times,
Elling

messages.body_plain:
Elling

You have the correct syntax for using covariates in the detection function; including your most complex example with three covariates.

However, there are a number of cautions I put forward for using covariates:
identify whether each covariate should be treated as continuous or factor (factors have discrete levels)
with factor covariates, the number of parameters to be fitting can grow rapidly, use care
likewise with multiple factor covariates, there can arise situations in which combinations do not arise in your data (observer B didn't make any detections in sea state 4); that will create fitting problems
finally recognise the pooling robustness property of conventional distance sampling estimation (where g(0)=1).  Distance sampling will produce unbiased estimates of abundance even if there are sources of variation in detectability you do not include in your model.  This is quite different from mark-recapture estimation where bias can arise in estimates when there is unmodelled heterogeneity.
if you are using double platform (mark recapture distance sampling) to estimate g(0), then you must include factors affecting detectability, however the example calls to ds() you provide do not suggest you are performing this type of analysis.

messages.body_plain:
Elling

I can't give a diagnosis without looking over your data, but ...

Addition of covariates might improve the AIC score, but often the effect upon the point estimates and the measures of precision are minimal.
If departures in fit are at large distances, one possible remediation might be more severe truncation as there is little information in detections at large distance about the shape of the detection function near the transect.
Little to say about lack of fit--do you have a quite large (>300) number of detections?  Perhaps with large sample size the tests have high power to detect small departures in fit.

messages.body_plain:
Elling

Recognise that by changing the truncation distance, you are changing the data set (removing detections).  By changing the data sets, the AIC scores between different truncation distances are not comparable.

There are no hard and fast rules regarding the "correct" truncation distance.  Section 5.3.1 of Buckland et al. (2001) mentions "selecting w (truncation distance) such that g(w) is approximately 0.15".  When including covariates, truncation might be increased a bit more.

messages.body_plain:
Hello All,
    I run (and often re-run) Distance on data A LOT.  So for me the detailed output, while useful for understanding one analysis, slows down comparisons across years.  I am working with data from 2-4 parks per year, where we estimate density trends using spotlighting.  We use the same methods on the same routes every 2-3 years.  I am working my way back through 20 years of this data.  I find errors or decide to look more closely at truncation or binning, etc., and I invariably need to run the model again.  Then I have to extract the same 20 numbers that allow me to look at density estimates, abundance, and group size across years.
    This year, I finally broke down and wrote a function to extract these numbers.  As you will see, if you are interested enough to read my clunky function, the values I need are not easy to find in the output.  This is one of the things that kept me from writing the function.  Don't get me wrong, the Distance package is great.  It does a ton of work and has really useful data in its output, serving a lot of different needs.  However, writing the function made me think that there may be demand out there for something that pulls the kind of data out that I have been gathering.
    I thought I would ask people whether they could use something like this.
    How can this be done?  There are already summary and print methods and a summarize_ds_models function that does some of this, but these are mostly formatted text outputs.  I think that currently, one way to do this would be to create broom::tidy and glance methods for R Distance.  If you are not familiar these are methods for grabbing, in the case of tidy, parameters that are commonly recorded or reported for an analysis.  In the case of glance methods, a one row summary of the critical outputs, perhaps ones that tell you whether your model fits or not, so for us, GOF p value and maybe CV of D, A, S, and p estimates.  broom also typically implements a augment method to add data to the original data table.  I cannot see a use for this, but maybe someone else can.
    What I need is "tidy" output with a row for each whole model output for a year and a row for each route within year.  My function does what I need for now.
    Let me know what you think about all this.  If there is interest, maybe we can turn this into a set of "tidy" summaries.
     -Pat

# Function requires Distance and dplyr packages be installed (not loaded)
# By Pat Lorch
ds_pull_model_params1 = function(ds_model = sample_ds_model,
                                 All = T,
                                 Year = 2014,
                                 Reservation = "Brecksville",
                                 ci_range = 95,
                                 Covariates = "",
                                 Comments = ""){
  # define a data frame with types we want
  ds_output_start = data.frame(id = integer(),
                               modeling_method = character(),
                               management_season = character(),
                               year = integer(),
                               reservation = character(), routes = character(),
                               n_params = integer(),
                               covariates = character(),
                               N = numeric(),
                               expected_S = numeric(),
                               area = numeric(), length = numeric(),
                               key_function = character(),
                               series_expansion = character(),
                               series_expansion_order = integer(),
                               left_truncate = integer(), right_truncate = integer(),
                               D = numeric(), D_lcl = numeric(), D_ucl = numeric(), D_CV = numeric(),
                               P = numeric(), P_lcl = numeric(), P_ucl = numeric(), P_CV = numeric(),
                               GOF_Chi_p = numeric(),
                               AIC = numeric(),
                               ESW = numeric(),
                               comments = character(),
                               date = character())

  half_alpha = 1 - (1-ci_range/100)/2 # For calculating confidence intervals
  ci_mult = qnorm(half_alpha)

  # Some stuff will be NULL, since not all models have all variables
  if((All == T & is.null(ds_model$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj$adjustment)) |
     (All == F & is.null(ds_model$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj$adjustment))){
    ser_expan = ""
    ser_expan_ord = NA
  }
  else {
    ser_expan = ds_model$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj$adjustment$series
    ser_expan = dplyr::case_when(ser_expan == "cos" ~ "cosine",
                                 ser_expan== "poly" ~ "polynomial",
                                 ser_expan== "herm" ~ "hermite",
                                 TRUE ~ "")
    ser_expan_ord = ds_model$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj$adjustment$order
  }

  if(All){
    ds_output = rbind(ds_output_start,
                      data.frame(id = NA,
                                 modeling_method = "R Distance (ds)",
                                 management_season = paste0(substr(Year,3,4), "-",
                                                            as.integer(substr(Year,3,4))+1),
                                 year = Year,
                                 reservation = Reservation,
                                 routes = "All",
                                 n_params = length(ds_model$ddf$ds$par),
                                 covariates = Covariates,
                                 N = ds_model$ddf$Nhat,
                                 expected_S = ds_model$dht$Expected.S[ds_model$dht$Expected.S$Region == 'Total',2],
                                 area = dplyr::last(ds_model$dht$individuals$summary$Area),
                                 length = dplyr::last(ds_model$dht$individuals$summary$Effort),
                                 key_function = sapply(strsplit(ds_model$ddf$name.message," "), `[`, 1), # get just first part
                                 series_expansion = ser_expan,
                                 series_expansion_order = ser_expan_ord,
                                 left_truncate = ds_model$ddf$meta.data$int.range[1],
                                 right_truncate = ds_model$ddf$meta.data$int.range[2],
                                 D = dplyr::last(ds_model$dht$individuals$D$Estimate),
                                 D_lcl = dplyr::last(ds_model$dht$individuals$D$lcl),
                                 D_ucl = dplyr::last(ds_model$dht$individuals$D$ucl),
                                 D_CV = dplyr::last(ds_model$dht$individuals$D$cv),
                                 P = summary(ds_model$ddf)$average.p,
                                 P_lcl = summary(ds_model$ddf)$average.p -
                                   ci_mult * summary(ds_model$ddf)$average.p.se <http://average.p.se>[1,1],
                                 P_ucl = summary(ds_model$ddf)$average.p +
                                   ci_mult * summary(ds_model$ddf)$average.p.se <http://average.p.se>[1,1],
                                 P_CV = sqrt(summary(ds_model$ddf)$n) *
                                   summary(ds_model$ddf)$average.p.se <http://average.p.se>[1,1]/
                                   summary(ds_model$ddf)$average.p,
                                 GOF_Chi_p= Distance::ds.gof(ds_model,qq = F)$chisquare$chi1$p,
                                 AIC = AIC(ds_model)$AIC,
                                 ESW =  dplyr::last(ds_model$dht$Expected.S$Expected.S),
                                 comments = Comments,
                                 date = paste0(Year,"-11-15") # set arbitraily at 11/15/year
                      ))

  }
  else {
    i = 0
    for(rt in unique(ds_model$ddf$data$Region.Label)){
      i = i + 1
      ds_output = rbind(ds_output_start,
                        data.frame(id = NA,
                                   modeling_method = "R Distance (ds)",
                                   management_season = paste0(substr(Year,3,4), "-",
                                                              as.integer(substr(Year,3,4))+1),
                                   year = Year,
                                   reservation = Reservation,
                                   routes = rt,
                                   n_params = length(ds_model$ddf$ds$par),
                                   covariates = Covariates,
                                   N = NA,
                                   expected_S = ds_model$dht$Expected.S[ds_model$dht$Expected.S$Region == rt,2],
                                   area = ds_model$dht$individuals$summary$Area[i],
                                   length = ds_model$dht$individuals$summary$Effort[i],
                                   key_function = sapply(strsplit(ds_model$ddf$name.message," "), `[`, 1), # get just first part
                                   series_expansion = ser_expan,
                                   series_expansion_order = ser_expan_ord,
                                   left_truncate = ds_model$ddf$meta.data$int.range[1],
                                   right_truncate = ds_model$ddf$meta.data$int.range[2],
                                   D = ds_model$dht$individuals$D$Estimate[i],
                                   D_lcl = ds_model$dht$individuals$D$lcl[i],
                                   D_ucl = ds_model$dht$individuals$D$ucl[i],
                                   D_CV = ds_model$dht$individuals$D$cv[i],
                                   P = NA,
                                   P_lcl = NA,
                                   P_ucl = NA,
                                   P_CV = NA,
                                   GOF_Chi_p= NA,
                                   AIC = NA,
                                   ESW =  ds_model$dht$Expected.S$Expected.S[i],
                                   comments = Comments,
                                   date = paste0(Year,"-11-15") # set arbitraily at 11/15/year
                        ))
      ds_output_start = ds_output
    }
  }

  return(tibble::as_tibble(ds_output))
  # return(ds_output)
}

8-12 June 2020, 1700-1900 BST // 1200-1400 EDT // 0900-1100 PDT

As a replacement for the usual advanced distance sampling workshop here
in St Andrews, we're offering the components of the workshop online this
year. This course will cover how to fit spatial models to distance
sampling data ("density surface modelling") in R. This will include:

- Generalized additive models
- Fitting, checking and selecting density surface models
- Predicting abundance
- Making maps

Examples will be based around a line transect survey of sperm whales in
the western Atlantic.

videoconference. Between these sessions there will be practical R

and discussion of practical exercises.

additional course later in the year (please e-mail to register your
interest, especially if this time of day doesn't suit you or if you
would be interested in a point transect-focussed course).

You should already know about distance sampling, for example by having
taken an introductory workshop in person or online (either interactively
or via our free pre-recorded lectures). You should also have some basic
R knowledge.

Prior to the course we will running a software test meeting to ensure
everyone can participate satisfactorily.

Mitch

Mitch

You are right to scratch your head when performing the calculations in Section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001).  Because with a pooled detection function there are parameters of only a single detection function to estimate rather than two sets of parameters.  That can result in some reduction in uncertainty, but in most line transect survey situations that reduction is modest, because the greatest proportion of uncertainty in density estimates derive from variability in encounter rates between transects.

Use of the Sattherthwaite correction makes a difference in the calculations when there are a small number of transects.  Hopefully, if you are in the design stage, you can design to have a sufficient number of replicate transects.

messages.body_plain:
Antonela

Thanks for sending along your data.  I believe you had a error in the data file.  Two of your transects, Salinilla and ypf had no detections.  In this situation, you should enter a value of "NA" for distance rather than 0, as you had done.  Line 3 of the code below makes that corrections.

With that fix, the "No models could be fitted." problem disappears.

I've fitted models with size as a covariate and with stratum as a covariate, neither provide a better model for the data than a model with a pooled detection function between strata and no group size effect.  There is a noticeable lack of detections at distances <100, but the fit of the half normal model is adequate as it smooths through the vacuum of detections at small distances.

library(Distance)
an10 <- read.csv("C:/Users/erexs/Downloads/2010_aniales.csv")
an10$distance <- ifelse(an10$distance==0 & an10$size==0,
                        NA, an10$distance)
an.10.size <- ds(an10, key="hn", truncation= 650, convert.units = 0.001,
                  adjustment = NULL, formula=~size)
an.10 <- ds(an10, key="hn", truncation= 650, convert.units = 0.001,
                 adjustment = NULL)
an.10.strata <- ds(an10, key="hn", truncation= 650, convert.units = 0.001,
                 adjustment = NULL, formula=~Region.Label)
AIC(an.10.size, an.10, an.10.strata)
gof_ds(an.10)
small.breaks <- c(seq(from=0,to=100,by=25), seq(from=100,to=650, by=50))
plot(an.10, breaks=small.breaks)
summary(an.10)

Eric Rexstad

messages.body_plain:
Antonela

The size of the P-value for goodness of fit tests is not a model selection criterion.  As long as the fit of the model is adequate (i.e. P-value > 0.05 or so) it is a suitable candidate for consideration.  Then, use the AIC score to determine the most appropriate model among those with adequate fit.

If the data are of good quality and delta-AIC scores are small, there is usually little difference in the estimated abundance from competing models.

Eric Rexstad

Thanks Eric, I think I’ve sorted the calculations out but I’m hoping you can help resolve my confusion regarding interpretation of the results:

When using the equations in the Introduction to Distance Sampling Section 3.6.5 for estimating a change in density for independent estimates (Buckland et al. 2001), the difference between estimates becomes significant when the second abundance estimate drops 14% compared to the first (when both estimates have a CV of %5 and df=30)...

I’m also interested in power analysis for the same research and compared these results to Fig 5.6a from Advanced Distance Sampling (Buckland et al. 2004). When the R code is adjusted to include an annual rate of change of up to  50%, it is estimated that between 4 and 5 years of data at a CV of 5% is required to detect a log-linear population trend of 0.5 per year (power = 0.8, alpha = 0.05).  I understand that the comparison of two values (mentioned above) and a power analysis are asking two different questions but it seems that the results are somewhat dissimilar.  I know that the power analysis includes an uncertainty in regards to the ability to measure the actual abundance, but the need for 4 or 5 years of data to detect an annual population change rate of 0.5 seems overly conservative.  Can someone please explain this discrepancy or point me to the error in my ways?

Thanks,

Mitch

Best wishes,

Mark

I have some bird survey data whereby an observer walked a 1km transect, within a 1km2 area, and record breeding species within 100m of the line. So I'm guessing this is a strip transect? Having looked at the on-line notes, am I correct to assume there is nothing that can be done regarding the calculation of detectability here? I would like to generate P_average per species. I have some covariates such as replicate number, weather and observer.

I have tried to fit a detection function as follows:

# Generate half normal detection function

  cutpoints = c(0,100),
  key = "hn")

Anthony

You are correct.  This is not really a distance sampling application, because you have not recorded distances.  Instead, you have simply not recorded detections beyond the truncation distance of 100m.  Estimation of detection probability requires information on distances as requisite information upon which the detection probability is calculated.

The survey design and protocol you describe does not permit estimation of P_a.  Happy you "smelled a rat" examining the measure of precision in the output from ds(); I'm a bit surprised and disappointed it didn't give up entirely.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm new at Distance Software and I would like to ask you some doubts about how to analyze the data from a line transect survey with Distance software. We collected the data of  moor macaque population in South Sulawesi by walking 1km transect twice. We were recording every time we saw an individual the distance from the transect, furthermore we were recording data about human activity (presence of humans, presence of animals (dogs or cows), logging (area), constructions, agriculture). Now I'm trying to analyze the data with Distance software but I'm struggeling with some issues, and I would be very happy if someone could help with that :). Thanks a lot!

 - We want to analyze if the presence of the human activity has an effect on the population density, is it possible to estimate population density taking in account this data? Is it a good idea to do it by stratification? i.e. stratify the data on "human presence/not presence" or "agriculture/not agriculture". Is is possible to do multi-stratification analysis?

- Is it better to analyze this data (human activity) as "covariates"?

- We have also some problem with the group size. We recorded every time we saw an individual, but we know that we missed some animals every time. We want to add a multiplier to accurate the estimation. We know the mean size of the groups in this species, and we have the number of individuals we saw every time we found a group. We think that adding a multiplier ("c"), where c = proportion of individuals missing, would be a good approach. If we see a mean of 10 individuals per group, and we know that the groups are abouut 40 individuals, we know we are missing 30 individuals each time, so c = 0.75. Do you think it is a good approach?

Thanks a lot for your help and time,
Best,
Víctor

messages.body_plain:
Victor

A good set of questions, I'll address them in sequence.
Effect of human activity
If you had designed your survey to address this question, then you would have defined strata on the basis of human activity.  You would then have allocated survey effort (transects) into the strata adequately such that you could produce robust estimates of macaque abundance in each stratum.  I'm guessing this was not done at the time of the design, but rather you are considering it post-survey.  The challenge with this is there may be too few transects in some strata of interest to produce reliable estimates.
The term "covariates" in distance sampling is usually associated with the idea of modelling the detection function.  While it may be the case that detectability is affected by human activity; you are interested in whether macaque abundance is affected by human activity.  The two are not equivalent.
There are other approaches to the assessment of the human activity effect besides stratification you might consider a spatial modelling approach where variables such as distance from village is used as a predictor of encounter rates adjusted for imperfect detectability.  See this paper applied to roe deer: Valente, A.M., Marques, T.A., Fonseca, C. et al. A new insight for monitoring ungulates: density surface modelling of roe deer in a Mediterranean habitat. Eur J Wildl Res 62, 577–587 (2016). Multiplier applied to group size
I am reluctant to recommend the application of a blanket adjustment factor to your survey data.  I would think the proportion of a group that is undetected would vary quite a bit.  Applying such a large correction factor would swamp any other decisions made in the analysis of your data.  As an alternative, Buckland et al. (2010) suggest recording the detection of each individual encountered, rather than trying to record the number of individuals in the group; analysing the data as detections of individuals rather than groups.  See Buckland, S.T., Plumptre, A.J., Thomas, L. et al. Design and Analysis of Line Transect Surveys for Primates. Int J Primatol 31, 833–847 (2010). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10764-010-9431-5

messages.body_plain:
Leo

Thanks for searching through the list; I don't think there is a general solution to this problem, because the introduction of covariates make even the question of detection probability challenging.  For example, you wish to know detection probability for each habitat type; that is an ambiguous question, because detection probability depends upon group size also.  So you must specify the value of group size for which you wish an estimate of habitat-specific detection probability.

Computing detection probability requires integration of the detection function (with appropriate set of covariate coefficients) integrated over all perpendicular distances (out to w).  I'm not sure that code exists in a general setting for multiple covariates, but perhaps more clever folks will show I'm wrong.

Rather than posing a solution to your detection probability estimates for various covariate combinations, I offer a mangled bit of code to draw pretty pictures of detection functions for combinations of a factor covariate with three levels and a continuous covariate of group size.  This approximates the scenario you described in your email.  I happen to have a data set for dolphins (provided with the Distance package) that I've tailored to suit our purposes.

library(Distance)
data(ETP_Dolphin)
nohelio <- subset(ETP_Dolphin, ETP_Dolphin$Search.method != 3)
luke <- ds(nohelio, key="hr", formula=~as.factor(Search.method)+log(size))
plot.with.covariates <- function(dsobject, groupsize, plottitle) {
  #   Purpose: plot detection function for each level of factor covariate
  #   Input:   object of class ds produced by ds(),
  #            fixed value of continuous group size covariate at which to evaluate detectability,
  #            title for plot in quotes
  #   Output:  plot
  #   Author:  Rexstad, February 2020
  #   Notes:   makes use of function detfct() to do the work.
  stopifnot(class(dsobject)=="dsmodel",
            is.character(plottitle))
  myobject <- dsobject$ddf$ds$aux$ddfobj
  truncation <- dsobject$ddf$meta.data$width
  mycovariate <- myobject$xmat[,2]  # position in matrix when only a single covariate
  thelevels <- unique(mycovariate)
  covar.levels <- length(thelevels)
  dists <- seq(from=0, to=truncation, length.out = 100)
  xx <- matrix(data=NA, nrow=length(dists), ncol = covar.levels)
  for (j in 1:covar.levels) {
    this.dist <- 0
    for (i in dists) {
      this.dist <- this.dist + 1
      tmpfilter <- myobject$xmat$size == groupsize & myobject$xmat[,2] == thelevels[j]
      if (sum(tmpfilter) == 0) {
        xx[this.dist, j] <- NA
      } else {
        xx[this.dist, j] <- unique(detfct(i, myobject, select=tmpfilter))
      }
    }
  }

  plot(dists, xx[,1], type='l', lty=1, ylim=c(0,1),
       xlab="Distance (m)", ylab="Detection probability",
       main=plottitle, sub=paste("For group size=", groupsize))
  for (more.levels in 2:covar.levels) {
    lines(dists, xx[,more.levels], type="l", lty=more.levels)
  }
  legend("topright", legend=attr(myobject$scale$dm, "dimnames")[[2]][1:covar.levels],
         lty=seq(1:covar.levels), title="Covariate value")
}
plot.with.covariates(luke, 200, "example with dolphins")
plot.with.covariates(luke, 300, "example with dolphins")

Possibly this can either provide visual information to address your questions or provide some hints as to how to perform the computations you might require.

Mitch, bear in mind that this is based on a t-test with just 3df for 5 years of data, and 2 df for 4 years of data.  So you are testing whether a slope differs significantly from zero on the basis of just 4 or 5 points, and for this analysis you estimate the cv from a very small sample size.  If you assumed the cv were known, or used the annual estimates of cv in your analysis, you would get very different answers.  The power calculation just estimates the cv from the departures of the estimates from a fitted line.  This is fine for a reasonably long time series of estimates, but probably not a good strategy for very short sequences.

Steve

Dayron

Yes, the Distance software cannot always save you from yourself.  You were suspicious of the data from Stratum A, and those suspicions were warranted.  Having only 14 detections is the first indication that results will not be reliable.  With none of those detections being within 30m(?) of the transect, you know you will not be abl to fit a deetection function with detection probability starting at 1 on the transect and declining thereafter.

Distance is following its instruction, namely trying to place a detection function throough the data you observed.  It has done that reasonably well, but in doing so, it has produced a ridiculous result, an estimate of detection probability of >20000 (rather than <1).

This reinforces the concept that you cannot simply take the results from Distance output and place them directly into your reports.  It also makes plain that you investigate not only errors, but warnings as well.

How should you interpret these results?  You cannot expect reasonable detection function fits to data that a) don't appear to conform to the assumption that detectability on the transect is perfect and decreases as a function of perpendicular distance and b) that consists of a small number of detections.

messages.subject_clean: Distance sampling software development plans
messages.body_plain:
Dear distance-sampling list,

Here is an update on our plans for development of our distance sampling
software over the next few years.  As you know, we have available
Windows software, Distance (http://distancesampling.org/Distance/),
which provides point-and-click access to a number of underlying design
and analysis engines, some of which are written in R.  The R packages
are also freely available (http://distancesampling.org/R/).

We recognize that many of our users are more comfortable using a graphic
user interface, and we plan to continue supporting Distance for Windows
for the foreseeable future.  However, we do not plan to add any major
new features to this software.  We will continue to ensure that the
software runs under current versions of Windows, that bugs are fixed,
and that the R packages called by Distance for Windows work as they
should.  We plan on making around one release per year.  Our next
release, Distance 7.4, is planned for May 2020; it will contain no new
features but the R packages included in the distribution will be
compatible with the new version of R (4.0) released at the end of April.

The major focus of our development effort will be on our R packages.

Over the past year, we have made some major improvements to the Distance
package, which provides a relatively simple interface for standard
distance sampling analyses (a feature comparison between it and other
packages is here
http://distancesampling.org/R/DistancePackageFeatures.pdf).  We plan a
new release, containing further enhancements, in July 2020.

We are currently funded (https://synergy.st-andrews.ac.uk/denmod/) to
develop enhanced methods and software tools for density surface
modelling, and these will become available as updates to our dsm
package, as well as to the underlying mrds detection function fitting
package and some associated utility packages such as dsmextra
(https://densitymodelling.github.io/dsmextra/).  We plan a new release
of dsm by the end of April 2020.

We are working on a new distance simulation package dsims that will be a
replacement for our current package DSsim.  One major advance is that
the new package will link with our survey design package dssd, rather
than relying on Distance for Windows (or some other software) to create
the survey designs.  It will have several other enhancements, including
a major speed-up.  The new dsims package will be available early in 2021.

We will continue to enhance and extend the suite of examples (often
called vignettes) available to showcase the features of all our packages
(https://examples.distancesampling.org/).

We hope you continue to find our software useful for your work – please
do contact us with any comments or suggestions
(http://distancesampling.org/contact.html).

Best wishes to you all,

Len Thomas, on behalf of the Distance development team

messages.body_plain:
The 2001 distance sampling book gives an example of a pairwise comparison.  This approach could be extended to more than 2 estimates.  E.g. if you have 3 estimates E1, E2 and E3, you could take -1.E1 + 0.E2 + 1.E3, find its variance, and hence test whether the value differs significantly from zero.  To test for curvature in the trend, you could take -1.E1 + 2.E2 -1.E3, again finds its variance, then test whether it differs significantly from zero.

There are no doubt other solutions!

Steve

you have sufficient computing power and begin with a relatively simple
model, this should work. It's worth starting out very simple (just a
smooth of 1 or 2 covariates) and time your model to see what kind of
time scale you'll need to work on. Code like

 > a<-Sys.time()

# run your model

 > b<-Sys.time()
 > b-a # obtain difference

can get you that number.

Hope that helps.

cheers,

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm using your new R package "dssd" to create a new design for a multi-national aerial survey of harbour porpoises in the western Baltic Sea (MiniSCANS II). I have nine different strata and managed to create a new design and a set of line transects (parallel lines with 10 km spacing) for these strata.
For some strata we already have existing transects from the German national monitoring (see here: https://www.bfn.de/themen/meeresnaturschutz/marines-monitoring/wirbeltiere/schweinswale.html ). For comparison with our previous surveys but also between visual and passive acoustic monitoring methods, we would like to keep these transects for these strata, however, we would need to extend the transects to the North to match the extent of the newly designed (and larger) strata. My question is if this is possible to implement in the package dssd.
I guess what we essentially need is to be able to set the starting point of the transects - which is random at the moment as I understand. If we could use the same starting point as the existing transects and then do the 10 km spacing, we should be able to generate a set of new transects, which fit the extent of the new strata but overlap with the existing transects, right?

I hope my issue becomes clear. Otherwise I'm happy to give more information. Many thanks in advance for your help!

Best
Dominik

---

messages.body_plain:
Dominik

I'm not sure I correctly understand your intention.  If your study area is the western Baltic, then you are not interested in the portions of the monitoring scheme in the North Sea, but rather strata I,J,K,L and O from the figure you cite in your email.

Furthermore, what you are proposing is to maintain the placement of transects in those strata shown in figure for consistency with previous work.  If you are not including random realisations of your design, then I'm not certain that dssd is the tool for the job.  The package dssd is useful for examining properties (such as uniformity of coverage) of various designs; accomplished by repeatedly producing realisations of designs.

If the locations of the transects are fixed (to overlap with existing transects), it sounds as if you only need to use a GIS system to extend the existing transects into your new northerly strata.

To my knowledge, it is not possible to fix positions of transects with dssd .  If I have misunderstood, I apologise.  Please clarify.
